extracted.intended_audience: Citizens of New York and voters considering ratification of the proposed U.S. Constitution
extracted.subtask_description: Explanatory/persuasive essays (Federalist Papers) evaluating the proposed Constitution's executive and Senate provisions, aimed at persuading New York voters. Discusses impeachment, appointments, treaty power, and the mode of electing the President and Vice‑President.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senate as court of impeachments (two‑thirds requirement protects innocence)
rubrics_metrics.description: The concurrence of two thirds of the Senate will be requisite to a condemnation, providing security to innocence; the Senate as a court of impeachments is an appropriate receptacle for that power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: two‑thirds requirement makes conviction difficult and thus protects the innocent; comparison with state constitutions where legislative branches act as impeachment courts supports appropriateness; consider historical examples and 'reason of the thing' when assessing fit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examine each power separately rather than vague aggregation fears
rubrics_metrics.description: When objectors claim the Senate will have undue power (treaty, appointments, impeachment), decisions should be made by examining each power on general principles, not by vague aggregate fears.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical method: evaluate treaty‑making, appointment authority, and impeachment jurisdiction independently to determine the best depositary for each power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counterpoises protecting House of Representatives' influence
rubrics_metrics.description: The plan provides important counterbalances favoring the House: exclusive privilege of originating money bills; sole right of instituting impeachments; ultimate authority in contingent presidential elections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These powers are intended to secure equilibrium between the national House and the Senate and may outweigh peculiar attributes of the Senate as sources of influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senate's role in appointments does not necessitate undue leniency in impeachment
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the President nominates and the Senate only gives advice and consent (ratify or reject), the Senate lacks a direct choosing role that would create strong complacency towards appointees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Senators may prefer other persons yet still ratify nominees; their limited agency and responsibility for the fitness of appointees make systemic favoritism an unlikely sufficient barrier to impeachments when serious evidence exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recess‑appointments clause does not permit President to fill Senate vacancies
rubrics_metrics.description: The clause authorizing the President to 'fill up all vacancies that may happen during the recess of the Senate' applies to officers whose appointments are not otherwise provided for and established by law—not to senators, whose appointment mode is otherwise provided in the Constitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Textual interpretation: consider clause connections, timing language ('during the recess of the Senate', 'expire at the end of their next session'), and explicit later provision granting state executives power to make temporary Senate appointments until the state legislature meets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Security against corruption in treaty‑making rests in joint agency and character of actors
rubrics_metrics.description: Confidence in faithful treaty formation is provided by the joint agency of the Chief Magistrate and two‑thirds of the Senate, whose members are selected by state legislatures and by the numbers and characters of those chosen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Impeaching two‑thirds of the Senate for a bad treaty would be as absurd as impeaching a majority of the House for bad legislation; instead security depends on selecting proper hands and making combination against the public good difficult.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electoral College design: electors chosen by the people as deliberative check
rubrics_metrics.description: The people should choose electors (an intermediate body) who will assemble and vote within their states; a small number selected for deliberation better analyzes presidential qualities and reduces tumult, cabal, foreign influence, and corrupting opportunities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Desirables: (1) people’s sense operates via specially chosen electors; (2) electors are capable of analysis and deliberation; (3) dispersed, transient electors resist sudden corruption; (4) eligibility exclusions reduce bias (no senators, representatives, or federal officeholders as electors).

rubrics_metrics.name: Contingency procedure for lack of majority (House of Representatives)
rubrics_metrics.description: If no candidate receives a majority of electoral votes, the House of Representatives will choose the President from the five candidates with the highest electoral votes, ensuring selection when the plurality is inconclusive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This contingency affords the House significant ultimate influence and serves as an additional counterbalance and inducement for electors to choose fit candidates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence of the Executive ensured by election and re‑election mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: The President's independence is promoted by making re‑election depend on a special body (electors) chosen for that purpose rather than on other branches, reducing temptation to sacrifice duty for those who control tenure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design rationale: making the President accountable primarily to the people (through electors) secures continuance in office on that basis alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mode of electing Vice‑President (same as President; preserves casting vote and substitution)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Vice‑President is chosen in the same manner as the President rather than by the Senate; this preserves the Vice‑President as an independent officer who supplies a casting vote in the Senate and may substitute for the President.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two considerations: (1) ensuring the President has only a casting vote requires Vice‑President not be taken from Senate seats; (2) Vice‑President may become substitute for President, so the same selection principles apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on presidential authority compared to monarch/governor (tenure, impeachment, veto, militia)
rubrics_metrics.description: The President differs from a monarch: elected for four years (re‑eligible), subject to impeachment and prosecution, possesses only a qualified veto (return for reconsideration, overridable by two‑thirds), and has more limited militia command than British king or state governors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating the executive's character, compare tenure, liability to punishment, nature of veto, and scope of military authority to determine whether office resembles monarchical power or ordinary executive offices in states.
